questions.q: Who is the poet of the poem discussed in Chapter 13, and what is the title of the collection from which this poem is taken?
questions.a: The poet is Nagarjun (नागार्जुन) and the collection is "लकड़ी का लक्खा". A wrong answer (e.g., naming another poet like Kedarnath Singh or a wrong collection) reveals the student has not read the introductory biographical note on page 130, which is the primary source for this information.

questions.q: The introductory note states: "कविताओं में 'खंडित' देने का कोई प्रयास नहीं है, इसलिए यहाँ कोई 'खंडित' नहीं दिया जा रहा है।" Explain in your own words what this suggests about the poem's structure and the poet's intention.
questions.a: It suggests the poem is written in free verse without artificial stanza breaks or forced fragmentation; the poet wants the words to flow organically, each carrying its own weight, reflecting a natural, uncontrived expression. A wrong answer that interprets 'खंडित' as 'broken' in a negative sense or misses the link to free verse shows the student is translating word-for-word without grasping the literary context of Pragativadi poetry's rejection of rigid forms.

questions.q: Nagarjun was actively involved in peasant movements and worked in the Hindi department of a university. Based on this background, predict two themes you expect to find in his poem "लकड़ी का लक्खा" before reading it.
questions.a: Expected themes: (1) Exploitation of the rural poor by power structures (landlords, politicians), and (2) The resilience or irony of everyday language as resistance. A student who predicts only "nature" or "love" themes has ignored the biographical clues about the poet's activism and the note's reference to "राजनीति और समाज में जो कुछ चल रहा है" (politics and society).

questions.q: Compare the description of the poem in the introductory note ("राजनीति और समाज में जो कुछ चल रहा है, उसे उजागर करने और विचार की दिशा को महत्व देने का भाव...") with the actual opening lines of the poem ("डगर कहीं तो रस्ता था घर के लिए..."). How does the metaphor of 'डगर' (path) and 'लकड़ी का लक्खा' (wooden measure) serve the poet's stated purpose?
questions.a: The 'डगर' represents the common man's search for security ('घर'), while 'लकड़ी का लक्खा' (a crude wooden measuring stick) symbolizes the arbitrary, unjust standards imposed by those in power ('मेज भरो' — fill the tables of officials). This metaphor directly 'उजागर' (exposes) the gap between the ruler's measures and the people's needs, fulfilling the note's claim of political exposure. A wrong answer that treats the imagery as purely literal (e.g., a poem about carpentry) misses the satirical layer the context prepares you for.

questions.q: The note calls this poem "हिंदी कविता का एक सशक्त और चमत्कारिक प्रयोग" (a powerful and remarkable experiment in Hindi poetry). Evaluate this claim: does the context provided (poet's life, movement, collection title) sufficiently justify such a strong label? Why or why not?
questions.a: Yes, because Nagarjun pioneered the use of colloquial Bhojpuri/Hindi idiom ("लक्खा", "मेज भरो") in high literary poetry, merging folk speech with Marxist critique — an experiment that was both linguistically daring and politically sharp in the 1950s-60s. A student who says "we cannot judge without reading the whole poem" is technically cautious but fails to use the contextual evidence (progressive movement, folk roots, anti-establishment stance) that the textbook itself provides to support the claim.

questions.q: Write a 3-line "context card" for this poem that a student could stick on the first page of the chapter. It must include: poet's lifespan, literary movement, collection title, and one key socio-political concern.
questions.a: Example: "नागार्जुन (1933–1975) | प्रगतिवादी आंदोलन | संग्रह: 'लकड़ी का लक्खा' | केंद्रीय सरोकार: सत्ता के मनमाने मापदंडों से पीड़ित आम जन की विडंबना।" A poor answer omits the movement or uses vague terms like "society problems", showing the student cannot synthesize the scattered contextual facts into a usable reference tool.
